alt: A comparison. Formal social control rests on written rules such as laws and school rules, enforced by police, courts, prisons, government, schools and employers. Informal control rests on unwritten norms, enforced by family, peers, colleagues, religion and the media through grounding, teasing or exclusion.
caption: Formal control is written and officially enforced; informal control works through everyday relationships.

alt: Three narrowing layers: socialisation, through which norms are internalised; informal control by family, peers, colleagues, religion and media, which keeps most people in line; and formal control, needed only when informal control fails.
caption: Formal control is the back-up: most conformity comes from socialisation and informal control.

alt: A two-by-two grid. Formal positive sanctions: medals, awards, promotions, certificates. Formal negative: fines, prison, exclusion, police cautions. Informal positive: praise, a smile, being included. Informal negative: a frown, gossip, ridicule, being ignored. Below, sanctions work through anticipation, and one agent can use both kinds.
caption: Sanctions are rewards as well as punishments, formal or informal.

alt: Four cards. Functionalists say control serves society by maintaining consensus and order. Marxists say it serves the ruling class by protecting property. Feminists say it serves men through heavier control of women. Interactionists look at face-to-face decisions by agents who label some groups, which can create more deviance.
caption: Structural views ask whom control serves; interactionists ask how it is applied face to face.

alt: Heidensohn argues patriarchal societies control women more effectively than men. At home through housework, the threat of violence, breadwinners’ financial power and closer control of daughters; in public through fear of sexual violence, reputation and separate spheres; at work through male hierarchies and harassment. Below, criticisms.
caption: Heidensohn explains women’s lower offending by control, not by nature.

alt: Two panels. Heidensohn uses control theory to explain why most women conform: patriarchal control at home, in public and at work. Carlen uses it to explain why some working-class women offend: the rewards promised by the class and gender deals fail.
caption: Heidensohn explains conformity; Carlen explains its breakdown.
